sentences.text: If the electricity that runs a heat pump comes from a gas or coal power plant, is the heat pump really any cleaner than the gas furnace it replaced?
It is a fair question, so let's put it to the studies.

The doubters are easy to find: one letter to the Boston Globe warned that "the majority of electricity in Massachusetts is sourced from gas- and coal-fired power plants", and the American Gas Association argues that a gas home can have a smaller carbon footprint than a heat pump home.

quote.speaker: Boston Globe

validation.text: A letter to the Boston Globe warned that most Massachusetts electricity comes from gas- and coal-fired plants, and the American Gas Association argues that a natural gas home can have a lower carbon footprint than a heat pump home.

contradicting.by: Deetjen 2021, private economics of US residential heat pumps
contradicting.note: Heat pump adoption raises CO2 for only 2.1% of US houses (1.7 million), but the estimate assumes grid CO2 emissions fall 45% over the heat pump's 15-year life.
contradicting.why: the verdict bears on the claim as worded

contradicting.why: the verdict bears on the claim as worded

contradicting.why: the verdict bears on the claim as worded

qualifying.why: the verdict bears on the claim as worded

qualifying.note: LBNL: fuel switching boosted carbon cuts (68% vs 50%) in the electrification cluster, but those projects were mostly in states with low-carbon grids, and the authors expect lower carbon savings where electricity is more carbon-intensive.
qualifying.why: the verdict bears on the claim as worded

sentences.text: So which is it, in real homes, on real grids?
Start in Britain, with households that replaced a gas boiler with a heat pump.

A working paper turned the change in those households' energy use into emissions and found, in today's terms, a cut of 1.16 tonnes of CO2 equivalent per household per year: 36 percent of the footprint their energy use had before the heat pump.

Add the qualification: the evidence supports a narrower or weaker statement.
issues.suggestion: Say where the narration carries this limitation (qualifications), or narrow the sentence.
issues.disposition: Scoped to the British homes; the coal-grid exception follows in s19.

resolved.explanation: In a video about replacing gas, 'average greenhouse gas savings positive in every state' will be heard as gas homes saving in every state, but Wilson's averages pool heat pumps replacing fuel oil, gas, propane and existing electric heating (the paper says so a page later, and reductions differ by previous fuel), so the cited passage does not establish the gas-to-heat-pump result in every state.
resolved.suggestion: Say what the average is over: 'averaged over every home, whatever it heated with before, oil, gas or electric', here or in s26's list of what the measure is not.

resolved.explanation: The 2.1 percent is of the whole US housing stock, whatever its current heating (Deetjen replaces each house's existing technology, oil, gas, propane or electric); placed as the answer to how many homes sit on the wrong side of the gas-versus-heat-pump line, a viewer will take it as the share of gas homes, which the passage does not give.
resolved.suggestion: Add 'of all US houses, whatever they heat with now' so the denominator is heard as all homes, not gas homes.

resolved.explanation: s19 re-tells s11 almost word for word (coal answering extra demand most of the year, Chicago, short term) and then s12 and s08 (both studies expect the case to grow as the grid cleans); only the pairing of the two studies is new.
resolved.suggestion: Point back in a short callback: 'Chicago is the exception, and both studies expect it to shrink as the grid gets cleaner.'

resolved.explanation: Knowing what your power company burns at the margin does not settle which side a house is on: Deetjen finds the outcome depends on the grid, climate, baseline heating fuel and housing characteristics, and RMI notes its short-term marginal measure ignores the grid changing over the heat pump's life.
resolved.suggestion: Soften to 'Know that, and you know the biggest part of the answer for your house.'

resolved.explanation: No passage ranks the marginal generator as the biggest factor for a house: Deetjen says outcomes vary by grid, climate, baseline fuel and housing, and calls current heating fuel perhaps the most important indicator of benefit; the studies here show the grid can flip the sign (RMI Chicago) but not that it outweighs the rest.
resolved.suggestion: Drop the ranking: "Know that, and you know the part of the answer these studies turn on."
